source_summary.design: Longitudinal three-wave panel survey (not preregistered), analysed with cross-lagged panel models (CLPM) and random-intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPM) in lavaan. It tests a Consequential Conspiracy Theories Hypothesis (conspiracy beliefs predict worsening health responses) against a Rationalizing Hypothesis (detrimental health responses predict rising conspiracy beliefs). The authors state that the longitudinal design cannot prove causality.
source_summary.sample: Dutch Kieskompas research panel. Wave 1: April 2020, first lockdown, N = 9033. Wave 2: June 2020, after the first lockdown, N = 6775. Wave 3: December 2020, second lockdown, N = 5745. Analyses use the 4913 respondents who took part in all three waves (3516 men, 1397 women; mean age 59.68). Models were fitted on N = 4118 because of missing values.
source_summary.measures: Belief in nine pandemic-related conspiracy theories common in the Netherlands in 2020 (credibility rated 1-5; alpha .84-.86). Physical distancing (4 items, 0-10). Support for lockdown policy (5 items, 0-10). Perceived danger of the coronavirus (3 items, 1-5). A second, 4-item conspiracy measure is reported only in the online supplement.
source_summary.main_results: CLPM, physical distancing and perceived danger: every cross-lagged path was significant in both directions, and the paths from conspiracy beliefs to the outcomes were significantly larger than the reverse paths (Wald chi2(2) = 81.48 and 173.62). CLPM, lockdown support: only conspiracy beliefs at Wave 2 predicted lower support at Wave 3. RI-CLPM (within-person change): conspiracy beliefs predicted a drop in distancing only from Wave 1 to Wave 2. For danger, perceived danger at Wave 1 predicted a rise in conspiracy beliefs, and conspiracy beliefs at Wave 2 predicted lower perceived danger at Wave 3. For lockdown support the within-person lagged effects were, paradoxically, positive. The authors conclude that the results support 'conspiracy beliefs predict health responses' more strongly than the reverse. Their last sentence: 'Apparently, conspiracy theories predict deteriorated health responses to Covid-19 throughout the course of the pandemic' (p. 5715).

occurrences.explanation: The substance is right. The source is a longitudinal study of 4913 Dutch panel members surveyed three times (April, June and December 2020), so 'three-wave Dutch panel study' is accurate. The quoted words appear word for word in the authors' closing sentence, which states the paper's own conclusion from its cross-lagged results. 'Predict' is the source's own non-causal wording, which fits the authors' statement that their design cannot prove causality. The problem is the page: the quoted sentence is on printed page 5715 (PDF page 7), not p. 5713. Page 5713 holds the within-person (RI-CLPM) results for physical distancing and the results for lockdown support, and the quoted words do not appear there. The deterministic quote check agrees: the quote is verbatim (score 100), but on printed page 5715. Optional note: the source opens the sentence with 'Apparently'. Its fuller summary also says the results were 'mostly consistent' with the consequential hypothesis and that within-person changes differed by outcome and by pandemic phase (for example, distancing changed only from Wave 1 to Wave 2, and the within-person lagged effects for lockdown support were positive). The waves span only April to December 2020. The author may want a hedge such as 'the authors concluded that', but the quotation itself is faithful.

evidence.quote: Apparently, conspiracy theories predict deteriorated health responses to Covid-19 throughout the course of the pandemic.
The present study sought to address the dynamic relationship between conspiracy beliefs and health responses on a large Dutch panel (N = 4913) at three time points during the pandemic
